item.title: Madrasah head accused of kidnapping student after she rejects his romantic proposal
item.description:
The director and headteacher of a madrasah in Gazipur’s Sadar upazila have been accused of kidnapping a Class Eight student. The girl’s father filed a case against five people at Joydebpur Police Station on Sunday night.

The prime accused is Ariful Islam, 29, who runs two madrasahs in the Joydebpur police station area and serves as their headteacher. The other accused are his brother, Sharif Mia, 35; their father, Selim Mia, 55; their mother, Rahima Khatun, 40; and a man named Delwar Hossain, 45.

Madrasah teacher beaten, handed over to police over alleged rape of child

According to the case statement, all the accused are from Char Bawla village in Mymensingh Sadar upazila. The student was in Class Eight at a girls’ madrasah run by Ariful Islam.

He allegedly made romantic advances towards her and harassed her in various ways. When she refused his advances, he threatened to kidnap her.

After the student told her family about the matter, they asked Ariful to stop such behaviour. Angered by this, he allegedly continued to intimidate and threaten them.

The case statement says that on the morning of 10 October, after the student arrived at the madrasah, Ariful allegedly took her away by force with the help of his associates.

Madrasah principal arrested over alleged rape of student

After learning about the incident through various sources, the girl’s father searched several possible locations. Unable to find his daughter, he eventually filed a case with the police.

The girl’s father said his daughter went missing after leaving for the madrasah, as she did every day, at around 7:30 am. He later learned that the accused teacher, Ariful Islam, had allegedly kidnapped her with the help of others.

Joydebpur Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Al Mamun confirmed the case and said police were conducting operations to rescue the student and arrest the accused.

item.title: Journalist murdered in Netrokona: Alif was targeted by criminals while investigating border crime
item.description:
A narrow, brick-paved road leads from the local highway into the village. A three-minute walk along it brings us to Robin Rangsa’s small shop, where he sells tea, biscuits and basic groceries.

Just a short distance from the shop, journalist Lutfozzaman Alif Fakir, 44, was shot dead at around 8:30 pm on 15 October. Robin was at the shop when the shooting took place. Last Friday, he recounted the incident to us.

Robin said Alif had stopped by at around 8:00 pm that night and bought six cigarettes. He sat at a table in the shop and smoked one before heading to his in-laws’ house nearby. Alif had been living there for about two years. In his haste to leave, he accidentally left his mobile phone on the table.

According to Robin, two other customers arrived and bought cigarettes while Alif was away. One was wearing a lungi, the other three-quarter-length trousers. A short while later, Alif returned to collect his phone and set off for his in-laws’ house again. Almost immediately after he left the shop, Robin heard gunshots.

Journalist shot dead in Netrokona

Robin was washing tea cups when he heard the gunshots. He looked up and saw Alif lying on the ground, with the two men still at the scene. Terrified, Robin retreated into his home behind the shop.

Asked whether he recognised the two men, Robin said he did not. He had never seen them before.

Alif was from Sunai village in Pogla Union, Kalmakanda Upazila, Netrokona. His in-laws lived in Telunjia village in Birishiri Union, Durgapur Upazila. A retired member of the armed forces, Alif worked as the Netrokona correspondent for the IP television channel Ruposhi Bangla. He also ran a Facebook page called Detective Article.

Through his reporting, Alif exposed smuggling, drug trafficking, arms-related activities and other wrongdoing along the border. He regularly published photographs and videos.

According to the police and his family, there had already been two attempts on his life. Fearing for his safety, he had moved to his in-laws’ house. It was there that gunmen eventually killed him. He sustained six bullet wounds to the head, neck and chest.

The day after the murder, his wife, Khadija, filed a case against seven to eight unidentified people. Police say Tajul Islam, 48, and Shamim Ahmed, 32, also known as “Shooter Shamim”, are among the leading suspects. The two men maintain separate networks of associates involved in illegal border trade, though they sometimes work together. Investigators are examining whether they helped plan or finance Alif’s murder and whether they had links to the attackers.

Alif’s in-laws’ house stands about 300 yards from Robin’s shop. After speaking with Robin, we headed there. Alif had lived in a small hut with tin-sheet walls. Among the old furniture and household belongings, a pair of blue trainers stood out. They had faded with years of use. His shirt, denim trousers and blazer had also lost much of their original colour.

Alif’s wife, Khadija Akter, belongs to the Garo community. The two had been in a romantic relationship before their marriage. She converted to Islam when they married; her parents had named her Anondita Sangma.

We found Khadija in the room where she had lived with Alif and their two young children. She told Prothom Alo that she initially did not realise the sound she heard was gunfire. She thought someone had set off firecrackers. Then a neighbour told her that Alif had been shot, and she rushed to the scene.

‘Feed the children and put them to sleep, I’ll be a little late’

Khadija said she lifted Alif’s head onto her lap and checked for a heartbeat. Having studied nursing, she understood that her husband was dead. She remained there, sitting beside him, until the police arrived some time later.

As she spoke, Khadija wept. She said the family had planned to move to Dhaka the following month, November. Her mother had even taken out a loan of Tk 40,000 to help them make the move. But Alif died before they could carry out their plans.

Crime Along the Border

Kalmakanda and Durgapur are neighbouring upazilas in Netrokona, both bordering India’s Meghalaya state. Smuggling across the border involves a wide range of goods, including drugs, sugar, cosmetics, blankets, cattle, machinery parts and firearms.

According to police and local sources, Shamim Ahmed controls part of the smuggling trade along the Durgapur border. Tajul, meanwhile, leads a criminal gang accused of extortion, smuggling and other offences.

Both men have been accused of involvement in a range of crimes, including murder, attempted murder, arms offences, drug trafficking, explosives-related offences, kidnapping, extortion, robbery and theft.

At least 25 cases have been identified against Shamim, filed at Durgapur Police Station between 2014 and 2026. Eleven involve charges of attempted murder, and 19 cases remain pending.

Shamim has also been accused in two murder cases. On 8 October, 2022, Subrata Sangma, a former chairman of Kullagora Union Parishad in Durgapur, was killed. His sister filed a case naming Shamim as the main accused. On 4 February, 2024, Shamim was again named as the main accused in the murder of Mojibur Rahman, known as “Dao Mojibur”, from Naljora village in Birishiri Union. The case was filed by Mojibur’s son.

At least 13 cases have been identified against Tajul. Ten were filed at Durgapur Police Station, while one each was filed at Kalmakanda Police Station, Netrokona Sadar Police Station and Darus Salam Police Station in Dhaka. The cases date from 2006 to 2022. Three involve allegations of attempted murder, and four include charges under the Arms Act.

Alif had reported on both Shamim and Tajul on several occasions. At least five people who knew him and were familiar with his work told Prothom Alo that he was determined to expose crime and wrongdoing on Facebook. Threats and pressure were not enough to make him take down his posts.

His Facebook page was one of his main reporting platforms. Khadija said Alif had gathered information about Tajul’s smuggling activities and weapons and passed it on to the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB). RAB arrested Tajul about four years ago.

Khandaker Shaker Ahmed, officer-in-charge (OC) of Durgapur Police Station, offered an account that partly supported Khadija’s statement. Speaking to Prothom Alo at his office last Friday, he said Alif had collected information about Tajul’s activities and published photographs and videos of his home and property on Facebook. Tajul believed Alif had also informed law enforcement agencies about the weapons he possessed. The resentment this created had led to an earlier attack on Alif, the OC said.

Shamim, too, had featured in Alif’s reporting. According to sources involved in the investigation, about a week before the murder, Alif posted a video that allegedly showed Shamim using yaba. Investigators are looking into whether the video prompted any fresh threats.

On 14 October, the day before his killing, Alif posted a brief message on his Detective Article page announcing that he would reveal evidence about a “godfather” of crime the following day. At 7:28 pm on 15 October, the same page published a 41-second video alleging that a man named Babul had played a role in resettling Rohingya people in Netrokona.

Investigators are examining whether either of these posts had a direct connection to the murder.

Threats, Cases, Arrests and Allegations of Torture

According to his family, efforts to silence Alif went beyond threats. Cases were filed against him, and he was allegedly beaten after being arrested.

Alif’s wife, Khadija, said that on 19 March 2024, Alif posted on Facebook about then Superintendent of Police Faiz Ahmed. He had planned to publish further information the following day. But the next day, men identifying themselves as members of the Detective Branch (DB) took him away.

The family alleged that police beat Alif so severely that he had to be taken to hospital. When he was brought before a court, he was still unable to walk properly.

Faiz Ahmed, who is currently posted in Khulna, told Prothom Alo by phone on Saturday that the incident had not unfolded as described. He said Alif had written about many people, including superintendents of police, on numerous occasions—not just that day. According to Faiz, Alif was arrested in connection with a rape case.

After Alif was detained, two cases were filed against him: one for extortion and another for rape. Documents obtained by Prothom Alo show that the case under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act was filed at Kalmakanda Police Station on 5 April 2024.

After completing its investigation, police submitted a final report on 11 April 2025, indicating that they had found no evidence to substantiate the allegation.

Alif’s wife, Khadija, said the case had been filed to harass him. She also said that after Alif wrote about smuggling along the border, Oli Ahmed, a local leader of the now-banned Awami League, filed an extortion case against him.

‘Police Officer Killed After Being Mistaken for Alif’

In one of the earlier attempts to kill Alif, a police sub-inspector lost his life. The officer, Mohammad Shafiqul Islam, was hacked to death on 9 January 2025 in the Panmahal area of Durgapur Municipality. A subsequent police investigation found that the attackers had been targeting Alif.

Mohammad Imdadul Bashar, an inspector with the Netrokona office of the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) and the case’s investigating officer, told Prothom Alo that two arrested suspects, Sajibul Islam, alias Apurbo, 21, and Mohammad Baki Billah, gave confessional statements in court. They said they had killed Shafiqul by mistake while attempting to kill Alif. According to their statements, Tajul had ordered the attack. Apurbo and Baki Billah were currently out on bail. Police believe they were involved in the attack on Alif.

Nearly 10 months later, on 10 November 2025, Alif was seriously injured when attackers struck him with machetes near the Teribazar ferry terminal on the Someshwari River. He survived. He filed a case naming two suspects: Samiul Haque, alias Sourav, and Mohammad Imon Mia. Both are out on bail. A charge sheet was submitted in September. Police suspect that they also took part in the latest attack.

At a meeting between journalists and the district superintendent of police on 30 November 2025, Alif spoke about the danger he faced, saying, “If I go out, they’ll shoot me.”

Sources involved in the investigation now say they have found links between the earlier attacks and the latest killing.

Six Names from an Old List

Durgapur Police Station maintains a list of 22 suspected criminals. Sources involved in the investigation say evidence has so far emerged linking six people on that list to Alif’s murder: Tajul Islam; Sajibul Islam, alias Apurbo; Mohammad Ashikur Rahman, alias Prangan, 19; Mohammad Sabbir Hossain, 20; Baki Billah, 20; and Samiul Haque, alias Sourav. Four of the six were allegedly involved in earlier attacks.

According to police sources, investigators have also found links between people close to Shamim and Tajul’s associates. They said they had obtained information suggesting that Tajul helped plan the killing while Shamim provided financial support.

Two people have been arrested in the Alif murder case: Sajibul Islam, alias Apurbo, and Ashikur Rahman, alias Prangan. Police say Apurbo is an associate of Tajul, while Prangan is close to Shamim and is the son of Shamim’s cousin. Prangan was arrested by SRB-14, the former RAB. Sources involved in the investigation said Prangan contacted Shamim after the shooting to find out whether Alif had died.

Officer-in-Charge Khondaker Shaker Ahmed said Imon was riding Tajul’s motorcycle on the evening of Alif’s murder. Another associate, Sourav, was also present. Investigators are examining each person’s whereabouts and role.

The source of the weapon is another key part of the investigation. According to police, the bullets used in Alif’s murder were 9mm rounds.

Shamim’s Brother Is a Union Parishad Chairman

Since Alif’s murder, Shamim and his associates have gone into hiding. Shamim is the half-brother of Abdul Awal, general secretary of the Durgapur upazila unit of the BNP and chairman of Kullagora Union Parishad. According to local sources, Shamim was previously known as a follower of the late Manu Majumder, a former Awami League member of parliament.

Shamim could not be reached for comment on the allegations. His half-brother, Abdul Awal, said political opponents were trying to tarnish Shamim’s reputation. Asked why Shamim and other family members were being linked to smuggling along the border, Abdul Awal said, “Others are involved in these activities, but our names get dragged into it.”

Tajul lives in Bagichapara, within Durgapur Municipality. He and his associates have gone into hiding.

How Far Has the Investigation Progressed?

Netrokona Superintendent of Police Mohammad Tarikul Islam told Prothom Alo on Saturday, “The group of killers is more or less clear. We are investigating the involvement of those who control the group. Two people have been arrested, and they are being questioned. We expect to deliver results soon.”

A special committee led by an additional superintendent of police has been formed to investigate Alif’s murder. Other investigative agencies have also been brought in. Alif’s mobile phone has been sent to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) for forensic examination.

Mohammad Zahidul Hasan, deputy inspector general (DIG) of police for the Mymensingh Range, told Prothom Alo that the investigation had made considerable progress and that details would be disclosed soon.

‘There Couldn’t Be a Better Person’

The Durgapur and Kalmakanda upazilas of Netrokona are home to several Indigenous communities, including the Garo and Hajong. Most residents of Telunjia village in Birishiri Union, Durgapur—the village where Alif’s in-laws live—belong to the Garo community.

Alif’s relatives on his wife’s side said he got along well with everyone. Members of the family and community considered him one of their own.

Alif’s mother-in-law, Shila Sangma, and his late father-in-law, Philip Rema, had three daughters and one son. Alif’s wife is the eldest daughter. Shila used to call Alif “Babu”. She told Prothom Alo, “He was like my own son. There couldn’t be a better person.”

After the July mass uprising, criminals operating along the Durgapur border switched political allegiances, but the criminal activities continued. Alif was attacked twice last year while reporting on those activities. In the third attack, he was shot six times and killed. Questions have now been raised about what the police did to protect him.

Haider Jahan Chowdhury, convener of the voluntary organisation Janaudyog and former district commander of the Muktijoddha (Freedom Fighters) Unit in Netrokona, told Prothom Alo, “We are stunned by the way journalist Alif was shot dead. Unless those responsible are identified quickly, brought to justice and given exemplary punishment, such incidents will continue to happen.”

item.title: Brazil's Lula defies odds to clinch poll victory against Bolsonaro
item.description:
TOPSHOT-BRAZIL-ELECTION-RUNOFF-VOTE

Brazil's leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round.

With Lula's victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries -- such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru -- all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.

The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term.

According to official results, he won 51.7 per cent of the votes to 48.2 per cent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls.

Bolsonaro clan wins big in multiple Brazil polls

Since the first direct election following the end of Brazil's dictatorship in 1989, no candidate who lost the first round had gone on to win the second.

Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula's Workers' Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.

In a video posted to social media, the president appeared jumping for joy,wearing red, star-shaped glasses, at a hotel in Sao Paulo, where he is scheduled to speak to the press later.

Flavio Bolsonaro, who is in Brasilia, has yet to react.

In Cinelandia Square, in the heart of Rio, Lula's supporters were moved to tears.

Julio Canelo, 42, a lawyer hailed a victory for "the entire democratic spectrum."

"It was the result of the people mobilizing, in the streets and online," he told AFP.

The left swung into action with massive rallies after the first-round defeat, declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro" and revamping a lacklustre social media strategy.

The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21 per cent to 19 per cent.

A bitter campaign marred by scandals and mudslinging laid bare the deep divisions that have remained in the country of over 200 million people over the past decade.

Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change.

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, pitched himself as more moderate and jovial than his father and managed to galvanize conservatives as well as less ideological voters fed up with crime, the high cost of living and a sense of stagnation.

"We're in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat -- buying meat is out of the question," said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro.

After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday's vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.

Lula rises again

Lula's re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast, in a family of illiterate farmers.

He rose to the presidency as a working-class hero, taking office for the first time in 2003. He was re-elected in 2006.

Revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.

The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.

In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters who turned to Flavio Bolsonaro felt gloomy about their economic situation and fed up with crime.

After a campaign marked by fearmongering on both sides -- many voters reported choosing what they considered the lesser evil.

A tricky term ahead

Already one of the world's oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.

He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as president from 2003 through 2010.

Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right.

His options are constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow.

He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant security problems in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighborhoods.

The president's campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump's United States.

Voters must "choose a country where the flag is respected," he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. He accused his rival of wanting to "govern with the American flag."

item.title: “My father has become the sky,” Muntaha says, pointing a finger upwards
item.description:
Two balloons float in front of the house. One is shaped like a chicken, the other like a shark. Four-year-old Muntaha Zaman Pranti says the chicken-shaped balloon is hers and the other belongs to her younger brother. Their father bought them the balloons.

Asked where her father is, Muntaha looks up at the sky. Raising one finger, she says, “My father has become the sky.”

Muntaha repeats that her father has gone to Allah. But she is still too young to understand that he will never return.

Muntaha’s father was journalist Lutfuzzaman Alif Fakir. On the night of 15 October, assailants shot him dead at Telunjia in Durgapur upazila of Netrokona. He was shot near his in-laws’ home, where he lived with his wife and two young children.

When this correspondent visited his in-laws’ home on Friday afternoon, Muntaha was playing in the yard in front of the tin-roofed house. She wore a red T-shirt and blue shorts. The curly-haired child had a smile on her face. The presence of unfamiliar visitors did not make her shy. She moved between playing and talking.

Her father’s memory is woven into this world of toys and play. Muntaha was the apple of Alif’s eye. He would indulge her little requests. She loved chicken fry. Whenever she did well in her studies, she would ask her father to bring some home. He would buy it for her on his way back. Her happiness was his happiness.

Toys of different colours lay scattered across the yard: a red rocking motorbike, dolls, a teddy bear, a plastic lion and a toy cooker. Open books and notebooks lay nearby, too. At one moment, Muntaha was rocking on the motorbike, gripping its handlebars with both hands.

Journalist murdered in Netrokona: Alif was targeted by criminals while investigating border crime

A little later, she climbed down and sat beside the toys. She played sometimes with the teddy bear, sometimes with a doll. She gently stroked one doll’s head with great care.

The shadow of a tree fell across one corner of the yard. Tin-roofed houses stood all around. Above her head floated the two balloons her father had bought. This yard is now where Muntaha spends her days.

Her father’s memory is woven into this world of toys and play. Muntaha was the apple of Alif’s eye. He would indulge her little requests. She loved chicken fry. Whenever she did well in her studies, she would ask her father to bring some home. He would buy it for her on his way back. Her happiness was his happiness.

That father is gone now. But the toys and balloons he bought remain. Muntaha’s little world is still filled with them.

Muntaha’s mother is Khadija Akter, a woman from the Garo community. She and Alif fell in love and married. Before the marriage, she converted to Islam and took the name Khadija Akter; she had previously been known as Anandita Sangma.

Journalist shot dead in Netrokona

With visitors at the house, Khadija brought out water, tea and biscuits. Little Muntaha seemed to take on the task of hosting guests alongside her mother. With her tiny hands, she repeatedly came forward carrying biscuits and offering them to visitors. Watching her busy herself like this, one could hardly imagine the terrible tragedy that had struck the family only days earlier.

Khadija does not know how she will manage once the money runs out. She is haunted by worries about how she will pay for her children’s food, healthcare and education.

Whenever Khadija spoke about her husband, she repeatedly broke down in tears. Muntaha sat beside her, silently watching her mother’s face. She listened as her mother spoke. At one point, when Khadija began to cry, Muntaha moved closer and pressed her little cheek against her mother’s. She stayed beside her. It is impossible to know how much she understands about her mother’s grief, but she would not leave her side.

Muntaha’s younger brother, Ayan Fakir Safwan, is only one and a half years old. He lay on a bed inside the family’s dilapidated house. He, too, is far too young to understand what it means to lose his father. When he grows up, he may not remember how his father held him in his arms or showered him with affection.

Now, with two young children to care for, Khadija is at a loss about what to do. The family had already been struggling financially before her husband’s death. Alif’s earnings from journalism had barely been enough to keep the household going. Thinking about their children’s future and the family’s needs, the couple had planned to move to Dhaka.

Khadija had studied nursing and intended to look for a job in the capital. The couple had been preparing to move there from November. To help them make the arrangements, Alif’s mother-in-law had borrowed Tk 40,000.

But before they could move to Dhaka, Alif was shot dead. All their plans changed. The Tk 40,000 they had borrowed to begin a new life is now the family’s only financial lifeline.

Khadija does not know how she will manage once the money runs out. She is haunted by worries about how she will pay for her children’s food, healthcare and education.

The man with whom she had built a home and dreamed of raising their children is gone. The responsibility for their future now rests entirely on her shoulders.

Four-year-old Muntaha understands none of her mother’s worries. She is still absorbed in her toys. Pointing to the two balloons floating in front of the house, she says her father bought them. And when asked where he is, she has an answer of her own: “He has become the sky.”

item.title: Cox's Bazar resort worth 'Tk 60m' demolished
item.description:
A joint operation involving various agencies and forces has begun to evict illegal hotels and resorts in Cox's Bazar.

On the first day of the operation, a four-storey resort building was demolished.

The building's owner claims it was constructed at a cost of around Tk 60 million.

Today, Monday afternoon, the operation was conducted at the building located in the Inani Beach area of Ukhiya, 26 kilometers away from Cox's Bazar town.

The operation, led by the Cox's Bazar Development Authority (CDA), involved the district administration, police, SRB, fire service, Department of Environment, and the Ansar force.

On the eastern side of the Navy jetty at Inani in the Cox's Bazar-Teknaf Marine Drive stands the star hotel Royal Tulip. On the northern side is another star hotel, Bay Watch. The four-story resort building is situated between the two star hotels.

Around 11 AM, excavation machinery (excavators) was brought in front of the resort building for the eviction operation. Workers also arrived. As the news spread, residents from nearby areas began to gather. By noon, 10-12 shops located below and on both sides of the building were demolished.

Then the glass windows of the four-story building were broken. The demolition of the main building's pillars then commenced.

During the operation, officials from the Cox's Bazar Development Authority (CDA) stated that the resort building was constructed illegally, and the owner was given four notices to demolish it on their own. However, no action was taken following the notices, leading to the demolition.

Shahidul Haque, the owner of the resort building present at the site, mentioned that the construction began in 2014 with permission from the union parishad.

Recently, several shops were prepared on the ground floor, a restaurant on the second floor, and several rooms on the third and fourth floors for tourists. The building, built at a cost of approximately Tk 60 million, was supposed to be inaugurated soon. However, it was demolished before that.

When asked about not responding to the notices, Shahidul Haque said, "I responded to all four notices. I have the paperwork about the building's construction, but no one is considering it."

Deputy Commissioner Md A Mannan Many illegal structures have been built on both sides of the 80-kilometer Marine Drive. Construction of structures, including resorts and cottages, is prohibited within 500 yards of the seashore in the environmentally critical area (ECA) and within 300 yards in urban areas. As a result, over a hundred resorts, cottages, and restaurants on Marine Drive have not received CDA approval.

On 17 October, a fire at the three-storey Tuptup Resort on Patuartek Beach in Marine Drive led to the deaths of 10 tourists. Following this incident, the issue of illegally establishing hotels and resorts without CDA approval along Marine Drive came to attention. Subsequently, a decision was made to start an operation to evict illegal structures.

CDA Chairman Engineer Muhammad Jasim Uddin said there are about 200 resorts, cottages, and restaurants on the 80-kilometer Marine Drive, mostly made of wood and bamboo without approval. Recently, notices were sent from CDA to remove these illegal structures. A joint operation is being conducted as these illegal structures have not been removed despite repeated notices. No illegal structures will be allowed on Marine Drive.

Muhammad Jasim Uddin stated that since the establishment of CDA in 2016, about 1,700 designs for building construction have been approved in various areas of Cox's Bazar district, including the municipality.

Construction on both sides of the 80-kilometer Marine Drive is prohibited. Nevertheless, around 2,500 structures have already been built, including approximately 200 hotels, resorts, and cottages, most of which lack legal approval except for a few star-rated ones.

Deputy Commissioner Md A Mannan told Prothom Alo that many illegal structures have been built on both sides of the 80-kilometer Marine Drive. Construction of structures, including resorts and cottages, is prohibited within 500 yards of the seashore in the environmentally critical area (ECA) and within 300 yards in urban areas. As a result, over a hundred resorts, cottages, and restaurants on Marine Drive have not received CDA approval.

The district commissioner said, "Without CDA approval, fire service, Department of Environment, and other government departments do not grant permissions. To ensure tourist safety, we are verifying the documents of various establishments, including illegal resorts and cottages. We are also conducting joint eviction operations against illegally established establishments."

In response to a question, the district commissioner mentioned that business owners have proposed setting up a one-stop service to expedite the approval process for establishments with some documents while lacking others, and their proposal is being considered seriously.

Regarding the eviction operation, Mukim Khan, General Secretary of the Cox's Bazar Marine Drive Resort Owners Association, said, "Several resorts and cottages have popped up like mushrooms on Marine Drive. We also want illegal hotels and resorts to be brought under the law because the tragic incident of tourists losing their lives in the Tuptup Resort fire has tarnished Cox's Bazar's reputation."

Khondaker Mahmud Pasha, Deputy Director of the Department of Environment in Cox's Bazar, said that 26 resorts and 10 restaurants were recently issued notices for operating without environmental clearance in the areas adjacent to Marine Drive. Fines have been imposed on 14 resorts, and cases filed against two resorts for not responding to the notices. The government declared the areas adjacent to the Marine Drive beach as environmentally critical (ECA) in 1999.

Abul Kashem Sikder, President of the Cox's Bazar Hotel and Guesthouse Owners Association, stated that their association has 187 members. Many of the hotels and guesthouses listed with the association have approvals, but he was not sure about the paperwork of the rest.

item.title: Ballon d'Or: Kane tipped to beat Yamal, Mbappe to glory
item.description:
Harry Kane is favourite to become England's first Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years when the award is presented in London on Monday, but he faces stiff competition from La Liga pair Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

Alexia Putellas is the clear frontrunner to win the women's prize for a third time, with Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign set to come to an end after an injury-hit spell.

The ceremony to decide the world's best male and female footballers is being held in London for the first time -- 70 years after England winger Stanley Matthews was presented with the inaugural award.

Bayern Munich and England forward Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double.

But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and at the World Cup in the United States mean a triumph for Kane at the London Palladium is far from certain.

"I'd love to be able to achieve something like that. It would be a massive milestone in my career," said the 33-year-old former Tottenham forward.

"I think my wife would prefer to know and my family... it's very stressful for everyone," added the England captain.

Only four players from England have won the Ballon d'Or. Michael Owen was the last to triumph in 2001, following in the footsteps of Matthews, Bobby Charlton and Kevin Keegan.

Bayern coach Vincent Kompany praised Kane's focus on his team, saying: "What made Harry happy the most in recent years is that he finally won his first team trophies here.

"Now if he can crown his career or his season with the Ballon d'Or, that would be deserved for the way he plays for the team."

''I deserve it'' -

Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d''Or winner one day.

However, a hamstring injury ended his club season early and he failed to show his most irresistable form during Spain's World Cup triumph, which was built on impressive teamwork.

But that has not diminished his confidence ahead of the ceremony.

"For me, Mbappe and me, we''re the two best players in the world," Yamal said last month.

"I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I''ve won."

Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France.

The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies.

His 10 World Cup goals in North America made him the top goalscorer in the competition's history, on 22.

"Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out," said Mbappe.

"Who am I voting for? Myself."

The Ballon d'Or was established by the magazine France Football, with the first award given to Matthews in 1956.

One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in FIFA's rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist.

Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player's overall market value.

Putellas, winner of the women's award in 2021 and 2022, was a member of the Barcelona side that regained the Champions League last season before moving to London City Lionesses.

Her former Barcelona team-mate, Poland's Ewa Pajor, is Putellas's main challenger after scoring 11 Champions League goals in Barca's latest triumph.

item.title: Blocking burial while in opposition, what will they do if in power, asks Tasnim Jara
item.description:
Physician and young politician Tasnim Jara has questioned the role of local leaders and activists of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami in obstructing the burial of freedom fighter Manik Pashari in Pirojpur.

In reaction to the incident, she asked regarding Jamaat, “They are blocking someone from being buried on his own homestead while still in opposition. What will they do if all state power falls into their hands?”

Tasnim Jara made these remarks in a post shared on her verified Facebook page and personal account on Monday morning.

Earlier on Saturday, freedom fighter Manik Pashari (87) passed away. He had testified at the International Crimes Tribunal against former Jamaat-e-Islami leader Delwar Hossain Sayedee in a 1971 crimes against humanity case.

Following his death, tensions arose over giving him a state guard of honour in Pirojpur. Local Jamaat leaders and activists demanded that he should not be buried there. They also staged sit-ins at several key locations in Pirojpur town. Manik Pashari was eventually buried on Saturday night in the graveyard of his own home in Chitalia village under Pirojpur Sadar Upazila, with his family members and relatives present.

Addressing the obstruction to Manik Pashari's burial, Tasnim Jara wrote in her Facebook post that in Bangladesh, when someone dies, there is usually no need to ask anyone to come and dig a grave. Once word spreads, young men from the neighbourhood arrive with spades. Some bring bamboo, while others bring mats. She said she had grown up hearing that the burial of a deceased person should not be delayed.

Yet, after 87-year-old Manik Pashari passed away around 10:00 am on Saturday, his family had to spend the entire day anxiously waiting with his body. Local Jamaat leaders and activists brought out processions and announced over loudspeakers and on Facebook that he would not be allowed to be buried in Pirojpur. Finally, he was buried late at night under police guard, with no one present other than administrative officials and his family.

Tasnim Jara said Jamaat leaders and activists spoke as though they owned the land when they declared that Manik Pashari would not be allowed to be buried in Pirojpur. It was as if a person needed their permission to be laid to rest in his own family graveyard.

She recalled that Jamaat members had once faced the slogan, “Jamaat-Shibir Razakar, ei muhurte Bangla char” (Jamaat-Shibir are Razakars, leave Bangladesh immediately). They should know how unjust such a statement was, she wrote. But, she alleged, they had forgotten that as soon as they gained some power, even while still in opposition.

She wrote that in 1971, Jamaat as a party opposed independence. Today, the leaders and activists of that very party want to dictate who is a freedom fighter and who is fake, who deserves state honors and where someone's grave should be.

She also accused Jamaat of failing to uphold justice, human rights, due process and human dignity for others, despite invoking these principles when defending its own leaders.

Regarding Jamaat leaders and activists, she wrote, "Before elections and in speeches, they speak of justice. Yet they treat a deceased human being and his grieving family like this. If they block someone from being buried on their own homestead while still in the opposition, what will they do if state power falls into their hands?"

Abdul Kader questions NCP's role

Abdul Kader, a former coordinator of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement, has questioned the role of Jamaat's ally, the National Citizen Party (NCP) in the Pirojpur incident.

In a Facebook post on Sunday night, Abdul Kader wrote that following such an inhuman incident, NCP remained completely indifferent and detached organisationally. Far from issuing a formal statement, not a single leader even uttered a word on social media. The deceased was known as a freedom fighter. In this case, the NCP sided with its alliance partner who opposed the Liberation War, extending silent support to the mob. Yet they claim to uphold the spirit of the Liberation War, and this is their example!

item.title: Woman who said ‘voted for BNP govt, now suffering’ in Facebook Live shown arrested
item.description:
Police have sent a woman business owner in Bhaluka of Mymensingh to court after showing her arrested under Section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The woman business owner was detained amid tensions involving local BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) leaders and activists after expressing anger against the incumbent government in a Facebook Live broadcast.

She was sent to the Mymensingh Chief Judicial Magistrate Court on Monday afternoon.

However, police have said that they found no anti-government remarks after reviewing the woman's Facebook Live video.

Bhaluka model police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Mohammad Zahidul Islam told Prothom Alo over the mobile phone that he had reviewed the woman's entire Facebook Live video four times.

They found no anti-government remarks or anything critical of the government in it. Such remarks fall within her freedom of speech. The incident originated from rumours because people did not watch the full video, the OC added.

The OC said that after the video was circulated, the woman behaved aggressively towards several traders at the market when they went to speak to her. This created a tense situation. For this reason, she was shown arrested under Section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and sent to court.

The market traders have assured her that she will face no problems running her business after securing bail and being released, he added.

At around 2:00pm on Sunday, Sathi Akter, 30, went live twice on Facebook from an account named ‘Sathi Makeover’. She owns ‘Sathi Beauty Parlour’, located at Khadija Palace Market in the Square Masterbari area of Bhaluka upazila.

In two videos, lasting 5 minutes and 22 seconds and 8 minutes and 8 seconds, respectively, Sathi Akter was seen expressing anger over a theft at her business establishment. At one point, she was heard saying, “We voted for the BNP government, and now we are the ones suffering.”

After the video went viral, local BNP leaders and activists surrounded her business establishment and demanded justice. As tensions escalated over the incident, police took Sathi Akter into custody at around 8:30 pm.

Mymensingh court police inspector Mustasinur Rahman said Section 151 of the CrPC is essentially a preventive measure taken by police. If police suspect that someone is planning to commit a cognisable offence, they can arrest that person to prevent the offence. In such cases, police themselves become the complainant and take the necessary legal steps.

The court inspector said the judge would decide whether the woman would be granted bail after reviewing the forwarding report submitted by police along with her to the court.

After examining the report, the judge may grant her bail or reject the bail plea, he added.

item.title: Mustafizur Rahman set to play in Australia's Big Bash League
item.description:
Rishad Hossain is almost certain to feature in the upcoming season of the Big Bash League (BBL). It has now emerged that Mustafizur Rahman will also play in the Australian franchise T20 tournament. The left-arm pacer has sought a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) to participate in the competition.

The BCB is also keen to grant Mustafizur permission to play. If everything goes according to plan, the left-arm pacer will play for the Melbourne Renegades in the Big Bash. BCB president Tamim Iqbal disclosed Mustafizur’s request for an NOC during the auction for the Domestic Three tournament on Monday.

Mustafizur and Rishad will miss the T20 edition of the D Three Trophy, scheduled to begin on 15 December, because of their Big Bash commitments.

There was little competition for Mustafizur at the auction. Seven Rings Cement, which secured him for 7 million points, will have his services only in the one-day edition of the tournament.

Shakib Al Hasan was the first Bangladeshi to play in the Big Bash. Rishad, the Bangladeshi leg-spinner who impressed for the Hobart Hurricanes last season, is also set to return to the same franchise in the upcoming edition.

The next season of the Big Bash is scheduled for December–January, which coincides with the T20 edition of the D Three tournament.

Mustafizur is not playing domestic first-class cricket after stepping away from Test cricket.

If crossfire is necessary and the government allows it, we will do it: IGP
item.description:
Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md Ali Hossain Fakir has said police will resort to “crossfire” if necessary, provided the government gives permission.

He made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at the inauguration of Community Islamic, the Islamic banking service of Community Bank Bangladesh PLC, in Chawkbazar, Old Dhaka, on Monday afternoon.

IGP Ali Hossain Fakir said police are labelled fascist when they use force, while they are called weak when they remain inactive. The police must be provided with a suitable environment to perform their duties and maintain law and order, he said.

“Where crossfire is necessary, if the government allows it, we will do it,” he said.

Referring to criticism of police conduct and the use of force, the IGP said, “When police baton-charge people, they are called fascist. But when police remain silent, they are called weak. Under these circumstances, the police must be given an environment in which they can work and be equipped to carry out their responsibilities.”

The IGP said the law and the Constitution must be followed to maintain peace and order in society. Police must take action against crimes, and members of the force must also face action if they commit offences, he added.

He also stressed the need for public cooperation in maintaining law and order. He said it was important to verify facts rather than be misled by rumours and misinformation.

Collective cooperation from all concerned was necessary to maintain normalcy in the law and order situation and ensure the country's economic progress, the IGP said.
