item.title: Who will regulate the race for deep-sea resources?
item.description:
The growing race to exploit deep-sea resources is raising concerns over environmental damage, fragmented international oversight and accountability, as countries and companies seek minerals essential for batteries and clean energy technologies.
Polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts and polymetallic sulphides found on the ocean floor contain nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. While these resources could diversify mineral supplies, large-scale extraction could destroy seabed habitats, disturb sediments and threaten poorly understood marine ecosystems.
The central question is who will prevent environmental damage in international waters and hold those responsible accountable when harm occurs.
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) provides the principal legal framework for ocean governance. However, responsibility is divided among institutions overseeing seabed minerals, shipping, fisheries and marine biodiversity, creating challenges in coordinating environmental protection and enforcement.
The International Seabed Authority (ISA) regulates mineral-related activities in the international seabed Area beyond national jurisdiction. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) develops international standards for shipping safety and pollution prevention, while the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) supports sustainable fisheries management.
Although these institutions have distinct mandates, their activities can affect the same marine ecosystems. The combined effects of mining, shipping and fishing may remain difficult to assess when environmental data and monitoring systems are fragmented.
An activity could comply with one regulatory framework while contributing to environmental pressures that another institution does not adequately address. Establishing responsibility for damage becomes particularly difficult when several operators and regulatory systems are involved.
The Agreement on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, known as the BBNJ Agreement or High Seas Treaty, entered into force on January 17, 2026.
The agreement establishes a framework for marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, marine genetic resources and benefit-sharing, alongside capacity-building and technology transfer.
However, it does not replace the separate legal arrangements governing international seabed mining, shipping or fisheries. Coordination among existing institutions remains essential.
Effective implementation will require credible environmental assessments, transparent information-sharing, scientific monitoring and action against violations. The treaty's entry into force does not automatically guarantee effective conservation.
The challenge is particularly significant for developing countries, which often lack the research vessels, seabed sensors, specialised equipment and analytical capacity needed to independently monitor activities in distant international waters.
Without reliable baseline data and continuous monitoring, determining whether environmental changes result from a particular activity, natural processes, or other human pressures can be difficult.
Unequal access to scientific research and technology can also limit developing countries' ability to challenge environmental claims and participate meaningfully in international negotiations.
For Bangladesh, the issue is closely connected to the health of the Bay of Bengal, fisheries, coastal livelihoods and the country's blue economy.
The Bangladesh Oceanographic Research Institute (BORI) is conducting research on coastal marine resources, potential fishing habitats and marine pollution.
Abu Sharif Md Mahabub E Kibria, a marine scientist at BORI working on environmental and climate issues, said the institute was researching potentially valuable mineral resources along the coast, identifying potential fish habitats and detecting marine pollution in coastal and adjacent areas.
BORI is also working on extracting agar and carrageenan from seaweed and identifying suitable areas for seaweed cultivation in the sea.
These activities could strengthen Bangladesh's understanding of marine resources and environmental changes. However, coastal mineral exploration and mining in the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction involve different geographical areas, legal frameworks and environmental conditions.
Bangladesh's exclusive economic zone is legally distinct from international waters, where the country does not automatically exercise direct regulatory control. Nevertheless, marine pollution and ecological changes can cross maritime boundaries, affecting fisheries, food security and coastal economies.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Department of Fisheries and BORI could play important roles in monitoring international developments, strengthening scientific research and representing Bangladesh's interests in global negotiations.
Expanding access to marine data, developing research partnerships and improving technical expertise would help Bangladesh assess emerging risks and advocate for stronger environmental safeguards and fairer access to marine genetic resources.
Ultimately, the race for deep-sea resources cannot be governed by a single treaty or institution. Effective oversight will depend on coordination among regulatory bodies, transparent environmental assessments, reliable scientific evidence and clear procedures for investigating violations.
The challenge is not simply determining who can extract resources from the deep sea, but ensuring that economic benefits are shared fairly, environmental damage is prevented wherever possible and those responsible are held accountable.
Earlier, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said: "International cooperation and effective implementation of the BBNJ Agreement are important for protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction."
Then again, Leticia Carvalho, the ISA secretary-general, said: "Environmental protection, scientific evidence and effective regulatory oversight are central to governing international seabed mineral activities."
Even, Qu Dongyu, director-general of FAO, said: "Sustainable fisheries management requires science-based decisions, responsible harvesting and action against illegal fishing."
Expressing his opinion to Dhaka Tribune, Professor Ainun Nishat, an environmental and water resources expert, said: "Decisions on deep-sea resource extraction should account for environmental impacts, scientific evidence and long-term risks rather than economic potential alone."
Energy and environmental specialist Professor Ijaz Hossain from Buet, said: "Demand for minerals used in clean energy technologies should be considered alongside alternatives, recycling and safeguards against additional environmental damage."
Talking to Dhaka Tribune, Abu Sharif Md Mahabub E Kibria, marine scientist at BORI, said: "BORI is researching potential coastal mineral resources, fish habitats, marine pollution, seaweed-derived agar and carrageenan, and suitable areas for seaweed cultivation."
University of Dhaka oceanography and fisheries researchers and BORI marine scientists agreed that long-term research and regular monitoring are needed to assess deep-sea biodiversity and ecosystem risks, where scientific information remains limited; besides, scientific data and regional cooperation are important for understanding how changes in international waters could affect marine species, food webs and fisheries.

item.title: Writ filed seeking halt to illegal sand extraction from Padma
item.description:
A writ petition has been filed with the High Court seeking to stop illegal and unplanned sand extraction from the Padma River, citing concerns over riverbank erosion, environmental damage and the safety of the Padma Bridge and its associated infrastructure.
Dr Md Golam Rahman Bhuiyan, chairman of human rights and social development organisation Manobadhikar O Samaj Unnayan Sangstha (MOSUS), filed the public interest petition on Monday. He is also a lawyer and human rights activist.
The petition raises concerns that illegal, unplanned sand extraction could alter the river's natural course, weaken its banks, and damage the surrounding environment and biodiversity. It also warns of potential risks to important national infrastructure, including the Padma Bridge.
It seeks High Court directives requiring the relevant government authorities to fulfil their legal responsibilities, investigate allegations of illegal sand extraction, take legal action against those responsible and implement effective measures to prevent further violations.
The Padma River plays a vital role in Bangladesh's economy, environment, agriculture and fisheries, as well as in the livelihoods of communities along its banks. Disruptions to its natural flow and ecological balance could threaten agricultural land, natural resources and the people who depend on the river.
The petition also highlights the need for scientific assessments and regular monitoring to evaluate the potential impact of sand extraction on the river and the safety of the Padma Bridge and related infrastructure.
MOSUS said the relevant authorities must take effective steps to protect natural resources, uphold environmental justice and ensure the rule of law.
Through the public interest litigation, the organisation seeks judicial intervention to ensure that the authorities take lawful and effective measures to protect the Padma River.

item.title: Living with the deluge
item.description:
As the monsoon winds down each year, the conversation around urban waterlogging in Bangladesh begins to fade. The rains eventually ease, the streets become dry, and the images of submerged roads and stranded commuters gradually disappear from our screens. Until the next heavy downpour brings them all back.
That is perhaps the most predictable part of Bangladesh's urban waterlogging crisis. Every monsoon, we go through the same cycle: Heavy rain, flooded streets, public frustration, a flurry of criticism and promises, followed by a return to business as usual once the water recedes.
What is missing is a sustained effort to understand why our cities remain so vulnerable and, more importantly, what can be done differently.
For a glimpse of what this cycle means on the ground, consider a familiar scene in Dhaka's Shantinagar neighbourhood.
For local shopkeepers, the heavy monsoon rain offers little relief from the heat. Instead, it signals a familiar scramble to protect their goods. Sacks of wholesale rice are quickly pulled onto higher wooden pallets, expensive electronics are moved onto top shelves, and makeshift sandbags are dragged to storefronts.
Within 45 minutes, the asphalt street became a stagnant urban river. Rickshaws pushed through waist-deep water as passengers lifted their belongings above it. This was a routine afternoon in July, not the aftermath of a super-cyclone.
Yet we have normalized this seasonal flooding as the inevitable price of living in a rapidly expanding metropolis. The problem is not simply the rain, but how poorly we manage it.
In recent years, the discourse in our cities has at least begun to shift. People are slowly moving away from blaming the clouds with a growing recognition of realities on the ground, that the aging drains and sinking ground are as much to blame as the sky. Naming the problem is merely step one; solving it is the real challenge.
The global North has embraced the “sponge city” model, using permeable surfaces, continuous mechanical sweeping, and underground systems to absorb and store rainwater. But importing this model into cities burdened by silt, dust, waste, and weak maintenance systems would be a recipe for quick failure.
If our concrete drains already struggle with solid waste, we need an approach suited to our own reality. That means moving from trying to keep water out, to a cooperative approach of giving it safe spaces to go.
Singapore turned this idea into reality at Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park. It replaced a 2.7 km concrete canal, once known as “ the long drain ,” with a winding, planted river through a public park. Its banks use roots and rock instead of concrete, allowing the river to spread across the park during heavy rain, slow down and drain without flooding nearby neighborhoods. In dry weather, the same space becomes a lawn for families and children.
What is striking is the cost. The greener river was about 15% cheaper than rebuilding the concrete, while carrying more water and the wildlife rose by roughly a third . Working with the water was the cheaper option whereas fighting it was the more expensive. That single fact dispels the excuse that this type of design is a luxury for our cities.
The global standard for managing overwhelming stormwater is moving away from rapid channelization and toward the creation of temporary flood spaces. In highly dense urban environments like Rotterdam, architects have pioneered the concept of water squares .
These are sunken public plazas that function as basketball courts, skate parks, or open-air amphitheaters during the dry months. When a heavy rainfall hits, they are transformed into massive, safe water retention basins until the city's drains can cope, then releasing it.
For Bangladesh, this idea can be adapted without the high maintenance costs of European-style public spaces. Imagine a school playground in Mirpur, a stadium bowl, or a neglected field in Chittagong, each built slightly lower than the surrounding streets.
Most of the year, they remain what they are: Places to play. But on the few days when heavy rain arrives, the surrounding roads can be graded so water flows into them by gravity rather than into shops and homes.
There is no pump to fail or imported parts to replace. Once the rain stops and the drains clear, the temporary pond drains away, and the children return. Accepting that a few designated places will flood is far more practical than pretending our streets will not.
Singapore's celebrated transformation of the Kallang River from a plain concrete drainage channel into a naturalized, winding waterway offers a compelling visual of ecological urbanism. However, our reality involves a vastly different socio-economic landscape, primarily defined by heavy solid waste pollution and informal settlements.
For 30 years, our answer to a filthy canal has been to roof it over into a box culvert and stop looking at it, which simply hides the silt until it hardens into a plug no crew can reach without breaking the road above.
The better path would have been the opposite, to break those concrete lids and daylight the channels back into open water. Researchers mapped this for Dhaka's Begunbari canal , but past attempts prove daylighting alone fails.
Hatirjheel was meant to be Dhaka’s Bishan , a decaying canal system reborn as a wide lake in the heart of the capital. Late last year it won a major international award. In the same season, the people staying beside it were holding their noses, because the lake had become a sewage pond.
Its treatment chemicals exhausted earlier and a waterbody the size of a small town is maintained by a handful of workers. The idea was not wrong, but the sequence was. The lake was opened before stopping the sewage flow into it, so it was already being poisoned on inauguration day.
When Seoul uncovered its own celebrated stream downtown, it refused that mistake and treated the removal of sewage as a precondition of the project, laying pipes to carry the district's waste away first. The result today is a green ribbon that cools the streets around it . Seoul cleaned the water, then reopened it. We reopened ours, then let it rot.
A daylighted canal will work only if cleaning is built into its design from day one. To prevent these canals from becoming open sewers again, we also need to make better use of one of our most overlooked urban resources: The informal waste economy.
Instead of relying only on municipal cleaning crews, the canals could be designed with simple trash traps, floating barriers, and accessible collection points. Informal waste pickers could then have safe and structured access to these points, helping remove plastics and other waste before they cause blockages.
Native wetland plants along the canal banks could further stabilize the soil, reduce erosion, and filter some surface pollutants. Together, these measures can reduce the pressure on already stretched municipal budgets.
In Singapore, water quality is supported by designed wetlands and natural filtration. In Bangladesh, we could also harness the people already working within our informal waste economy, giving them a safer and more productive role in keeping our waterways clear.
A significant but rarely discussed driver of our drainage crisis is the burden that unchecked private development places on public infrastructure.
Every new commercial high-rise or apartment block that covers its plot with concrete sends more rainwater into already overwhelmed streets and drains.
The solution is to make large developments manage more of their own runoff. Building codes could require blue roofs that temporarily store rainwater and release it slowly, along with underground cisterns to collect water for flushing, cooling, and irrigation.
This would reduce the pressure on struggling, underfunded city corporations and make private developers share the cost of the urban growth from which they profit.
Portland's breakthrough came from embracing the power of the small. The American city once struggled with severe storm overflows that dumped raw sewage into its riverways. Rather than building a massive infrastructure, Portland paid ordinary citizens to disconnect 56,000 rooftop downspouts from the municipal sewers.
By letting rainwater absorb into private gardens, the city diverted over a billion gallons a year from its overloaded network. This approach endures because it lacks mechanical complexity. In a country like Bangladesh where centralized machinery is often the first to fail and the last to be repaired, this decentralized simplicity is worth more than any monument.
Every one of these ideas runs, in the end, onto the same reef that wrecked Hatirjheel, our national habit of celebration with grand inauguration ceremonies, only to be abandoned to long-term neglect.
To break this cycle, we must look backward to traditional practices. Historically, the maintenance of local water bodies, ponds, and drainage channels was a communal responsibility, deeply embedded in the civic fabric of rural life.
As millions migrated to the cities, this intrinsic stewardship was completely outsourced to a faceless, sprawling bureaucracy, leading to widespread apathy and a disconnect between citizens and their immediate environment.
We should be able to revive this stewardship by formalizing community guardianship over neighborhood drainage networks. Instead of awarding massive maintenance contracts to distant corporate entities who have no stake in the community's well-being, city authorities could issue decentralized micro-contracts.
These contracts would be awarded to local neighbourhood cooperatives, youth groups, or even organized associations within the informal settlements situated directly alongside the water bodies.
Paying the local community a steady wage to maintain the flow and cleanliness of their own immediate drainage channels ensures continuous, hyper- localized oversight.
Surviving the harsh, changing realities of our rain-battered delta requires abandoning the idea that engineering alone can control water. We cannot concrete our way out of the monsoon, nor can we simply rely on importing green infrastructure designed for very different climates.
The goal is not to become Singapore, Rotterdam, or Seoul. Their climate is different from ours, their resources are greater, and their institutions work differently. But they offer an important lesson: Water does not always have to be pushed away.
Cities can be designed to hold it, slow it down, and let it pass. The challenge for Bangladesh is to find ways to apply that principle to our own climate, resources, and realities.
The rain will fall again. Shopkeepers in Shantinagar and many other parts of the country will once again move their goods to higher shelves, just as they have done for years. We cannot stop the rain. But we can decide what happens when it falls.
Somewhere in this city, a dead, black canal could, within a few years, become a clean waterway where children play beside the water and families sit on the bank on a pleasant evening.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad, a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy, now shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org.

item.title: Going cashless demands more digital security
item.description:
The near-doubling of payment cards across Bangladesh over the past five years -- surging to nearly 53 million cards alongside an even bigger leap in total transaction values -- signals a profound shift toward a more cashless, digitized economy. This is a positive, especially for a nation that has long aspired to more effective digitization.
According to recent Bangladesh Bank data, debit, credit, and prepaid instruments have all become deeply embedded in urban and retail consumer behaviour. Yet, we cannot ignore the fact that this rapid financial modernization brings with it urgent structural challenges.
While the proliferation of cashless options broadens financial access, it also exposes systemic vulnerabilities within our digital financial ecosystem. Consumer cybersecurity education, fraud protection mechanisms, and robust merchant infrastructure have not kept pace with this rapid adoption, and as more citizens transition to electronic payments, cybersecurity threats have the potential to undermine public trust in the digital banking architecture.
Furthermore, the widening gap in cross-border card usage -- where outward spending by Bangladeshis abroad drastically outstrips foreign card spending within the country -- highlights ongoing pressures on foreign exchange reserves and capital flight concerns, and cannot be entirely dismissed.
As such, the central bank, and our financial sector at large, must move beyond celebrating raw adoption metrics. True digital financial inclusion requires unyielding regulatory oversight and a cybersecurity apparatus that protects people from threats.
A modernized payment system is only as strong as its weakest security link. As such, it is imperative that we do not fail to guarantee absolute protection for digital transactions. The promise of a cashless economy only exists when those who are to benefit from it are protected.

item.title: We need good teachers
item.description:
We are troubled by a recent report in this newspaper revealing a deep-seated crisis in our government schools, where severe staffing shortages, acute leadership deficits, and an absence of subject-specialist educators are all but crippling classroom learning.
When over 27,000 of the roughly 65,000 primary headteacher posts sit vacant nationwide, and even more assistant teacher slots in secondary schools remain unfilled, the commitment to building a competitive, modern workforce rings entirely hollow.
When a handful of teachers are responsible for the education of hundreds of students, it is no wonder then that the standards fall. We cannot be blaming educators when they are forced to manage classes of such numbers while simultaneously burdened with tedious daily administrative paperwork
Compounding this structural vacuum, official recently published data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS) shows that over 52% of government secondary school teachers lack basic professional pedagogical training.
To that end, expecting understaffed, untrained, and administratively overwhelmed teachers to deliver high-quality instruction is an absurd strategy destined for failure.
This paralysis stems directly from bureaucratic inertia, prolonged recruitment delays, and an utter lack of strategic planning. While state officials frequently boast about digital initiatives and infrastructure expansions, they consistently ignore the fundamental pillar of learning: Qualified, well-supported teachers. Brick-and-mortar classrooms mean nothing without competent educators to guide the students inside them.
This crisis must be confronted with unyielding urgency. Stopgap measures and delayed hiring drives will no longer suffice. It is time to eliminate administrative bottlenecks and aggressively fill all vacant teaching and administrative positions.
Crucially, we also need rigorous, mandatory pre-service training and competitive incentives to attract better talent into the teaching profession, along with eliminating offering jobs to those who are unqualified.
Education will only be the backbone of our economy if we do not sacrifice the future of our youth to bureaucratic complacency regarding teachers.

item.title: PM apprises Japanese parliamentary delegation of steps to attract investments
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday outlined his government’s initiatives, including legal reforms, to create a business-friendly environment for foreign investors and highlighted measures to promote education and skills development during a meeting with a high-level Japanese parliamentary delegation. The delegation of the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League (JBPFL), led by its president and former Japanese prime minister Taro Aso, met the prime minister at Hotel Imperial in Tokyo at 3pm local time. Both sides emphasised the need to further strengthen political and economic ties as well as people-to-people contacts between Bangladesh and Japan.
During the meeting, the Prime Minister said his government had undertaken several initiatives to create a business-friendly environment for foreign investors, including legal reforms. He also outlined government initiatives in education and skills development. In the context of the proposed Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) between Bangladesh and Japan, Tarique Rahman sought Tara Aso’s cooperation in increasing Japanese investment in Bangladesh, expanding bilateral trade and strengthening technology transfer. He also expressed the hope that Japan would continue to support Bangladesh in implementing its development priorities and developing a skilled workforce. Tarique Rahman thanked Tara Aso for his continued contribution to strengthening friendly relations between Bangladesh and Japan through his leadership of the parliamentary friendship league. Tarique Rahman recalled meeting Tara Aso during his visit to Japan in 2006, when he was the senior joint secretary general of Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP). The former Japanese premier also recalled his meeting with former Bangladesh Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia. The premier said Tara Aso had consistently played a positive and constructive role in advancing bilateral relations while serving in various important positions, including as Japan’s prime minister, deputy prime minister and finance minister. His long standing personal engagement with Bangladesh had contributed significantly to further strengthening the friendship between the two countries, he added. Commenting on Bangladesh’s investment prospects, Taro Aso said a large proportion of the country’s population was young and that the current political stability had created a favourable environment for investment.
Japanese companies were highly interested in investing in Bangladesh, he added. Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M. Rashiduzzaman Millat, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Anindya Islam Amit, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology and Science and Technology Rehan Asif Asad, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Overseas Employment in the Asia-Pacific region Md. Shakhawat Hossen Rubel and Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon were present, among others. The Japanese delegation included former minister and Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) chairman Yasutoshi Nishimura, Japanese Minister of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism Tatsunori Ibayashi, and senior members of the Japanese parliament.

item.title: NBR raids Gulshan restaurant, seizes alcohol over suspected duty evasion
item.description:
A joint team of four intelligence agencies of the National Board of Revenue (NBR) seized a large quantity of alcohol and alcoholic beverages without valid documents during a raid on Kingfisher Restaurant Ltd in the capital’s Gulshan area.
The special operation was conducted from 12:30am on Sunday and continued for around three hours, following confidential information received by the NBR that highly dutiable goods, particularly alcohol and alcoholic beverages, are being procured and sold by evading duties.
The operation was carried out under the NBR’s directives and the overall supervision of the Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID), according to a press release issued on Monday.
The participating agencies were the Central Intelligence Cell (CIC), CIID, Tax Intelligence and Investigation Unit (TIIU), and VAT Audit, Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (VAIID).
The team conducted the raid to identify stocks of alcohol allegedly obtained through illegal sources and smuggling, prevent value-added tax (VAT) evasion on local sales, verify whether sales proceeds had been properly declared in income tax returns, and examine possible links between the transactions and money laundering.
The operation was conducted under the provisions of the Customs Act, 2023, the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012, the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Rules, 2016, and the Income Tax Act, 2023.
The Special Response Battalion (SRB-1) provided support throughout the operation.
The NBR did not specify the quantity or estimated value of the seized alcohol in its press release issued on Monday.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 4th among world's most polluted cities Monday morning
item.description:
Dhaka ranked as the world's fourth most polluted city on Monday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 168 at 9:30am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", indicating that the concentration of airborne pollutants had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general public, according to the AQI scale.
India's Delhi topped the list with an AQI score of 200, followed by Pakistan's Lahore and Karachi, with scores of 199 and 175, respectively.
An AQI reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while a score between 151 and 200 is classified as "unhealthy". Readings between 201 and 300 are deemed "very unhealthy", and levels above 301 are considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI, an index that tracks daily air quality, indicates how polluted the air is and the potential health effects on residents.
In Bangladesh, AQI measurements are based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and ozone.
According to the World Health Organization, air pollution causes an estimated seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Bangladesh reach two gold-medal matches at Asia Cup archery
item.description:
Bangladesh have secured places in two gold-medal matches at the 2026 Asia Cup World Ranking Tournament Leg II in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq, with the recurve men’s team and compound women’s team advancing to their respective finals.
The recurve men’s team of Abdur Rahman Alif, Md Sagor Islam and Abdullah Al Mohammad Rafi defeated Uzbekistan 6-0 in the semifinals to set up a title clash against Kazakhstan.
The compound women’s team, comprising Bonna Akter, Sriparna Biswas and Kulsum Akter Moni, also booked their place in the final after beating Sri Lanka 233-219. They will face Kazakhstan in the gold-medal match.
Bangladesh’s archers have impressed since the start of the competition, with the country topping both compound individual qualification events.
Nawaz Ahmed Rakib secured the top seed in the compound men’s event with a score of 693, edging Kazakhstan’s Pavel Kuznetsov. Bangladesh’s Himu Bachhar also finished among the leading qualifiers, placing fourth.
In the compound women’s qualification, Bonna topped the standings with 696 points, ahead of Iraq’s Fatimah Saad AlMashhadani, who scored 693, while Kazakhstan’s Elmira Raissova finished third with 685.
Alif also delivered a strong performance in the recurve men’s qualification, scoring 657 to finish third. Iran’s Mohammadhossein Golshani Asl led the standings with 670, followed by Nicholas D’Amour of the United States with 661.
Bangladesh’s compound men’s team had made history at the first leg in Bangkok by winning the country’s first-ever Asia Cup gold in the event. Rakib and Bachhar were part of that gold-winning team, which will now aim to defend its title in Sulaymaniyah.
The second leg of the 2026 Asia Cup is being held from October 24 to 29, offering archers an opportunity to win medals and earn valuable world-ranking points.
With two finals on Wednesday and Thursday secured, Bangladesh will now look to turn their strong performances into gold medals on the international stage.

item.title: Mustafizur set to play for Melbourne Renegades in Big Bash League
item.description:
Bangladesh left-arm pacer Mustafizur Rahman is set to feature for Melbourne Renegades in Australia's Big Bash League (BBL), potentially becoming the latest Bangladeshi cricketer to take part in the tournament.
Mustafizur, popularly known as the “Cutter Master” for his deceptive variations, has sought a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) to play in the Australian T20 competition.
BCB president Tamim Iqbal confirmed the development to reporters on Monday during the auction for the domestic D3 tournament, saying both Mustafizur and leg-spinner Rishad Hossain had applied for NOCs to play in the BBL.
Tamim also indicated a positive stance towards granting the duo permission to participate in the tournament.
Rishad, meanwhile, is set to return to Hobart Hurricanes after featuring for the franchise in the previous edition of the BBL.
The leg-spinner made an impression during his stint with Hobart last season, paving the way for another Bangladeshi player to feature in Australia's premier domestic T20 competition.

item.title: Kane primed to pip Yamal, Mbappe to Ballon d'Or glory
item.description:
England captain Harry Kane is the favourite to win a wide open race to be crowned Ballon d'Or winner at a glitzy London ceremony on Monday, with Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe also in the running to be named the world's best footballer.
The 70th edition of the award, established by the magazine France Football, will be hosted in England for the first time in recognition of the first winner Stanley Matthews and fittingly could have a first English winner for 25 years.
Bayern Munich striker Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, leading the German giants to a league and cup double and England to the semi-finals of the World Cup.
"I'd love to be able to achieve something like that. I would be a massive milestone in my career," said the 33-year-old.
But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and World Cup for Kane means the outcome is far from certain.
"I think my wife would prefer to know and my family ... it's very stressful for everyone," he added.
"I can see why they don't tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don't know."
- 'I deserve it' -
Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d'Or winner one day.
However, after a hamstring injury ended his club season early, he was far from the shining light of Spain's World Cup triumph that was built on being the best collective unit.
Yamal was pipped to both the player and young player of the tournament by his Barcelona team-mates Rodri and Pau Cubarsi.
That has not diminished his bullish confidence ahead of the ceremony.
"For me, Mbappe and me, we're the two best players in the world," Yamal said last month.
"I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I've won."
Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France.
The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies.
His 10 World Cup goals made him the top goalscorer in the competition's history on 22.
"Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out," said Mbappe.
"Who am I voting for? Myself."
One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in FIFA's rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist, allocating a maximum of 15 points down to one based on their ranking.
The Ballon d'Or goes to the player who accrued the most points.
Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player's overall marketing value.
Alexia Putellas is the frontrunner to win the women's award for the third time with Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign to come to an end after an injury-hit year.
Putellas, winner in 2021 and 2022, was part of the Barcelona side that regained the Champions League last season before moving to London City Lionesses.
Her former club team-mate, Poland's Ewa Pajor is the main challenger to Putellas after she netted 11 Champions League goals in Barca's latest triumph.

item.title: Salahuddin replaces Ashraful as national team batting coach
item.description:
The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) appointed Mohammad Salahuddin as the batting coach of the national team on an interim basis, replacing Mohammad Ashraful.
In a press release, the BCB stated that Ashraful will be reassigned to a new role within the Board.
Ashraful was appointed as the national team's batting coach in November 2025.
The BCB thanks him for his service and efforts during this period with the Bangladesh team.
Mohammad Salahuddin has been serving as the BCB's High Performance Head Coach but will be overseeing the national team batting until the Board appoints a new batting coach.

item.title: Real century 'just a detail' for Mbappe after Clasico win
item.description:
Kylian Mbappe said reaching a milestone 100 goals for Real Madrid during the 2-1 Clasico win over Barcelona in La Liga on Sunday was "just a detail" compared to the team's victory.
The French forward hit a brace to bring up his century for Los Blancos across all competitions since joining in 2024.
Mbappe's double, either side of a Raphinha strike for the hosts at Camp Nou, brought third-place Real Madrid within three points of the La Liga leaders and reigning Spanish champions.
"I'm very happy, I think everyone knows I like to score goals, I like to help the team with that, but I think today it's just a detail, because... the most important thing is the team's win," Mbappe told Real Madrid TV.
"Honestly, the real star of the game today is the team, the group, because we knew we had to play a big game, a team game...
"We know that in the end it was a great game, but it still only counts as three points, and we need to pick up a lot of points to win La Liga."
Jose Mourinho's Madrid have now won five matches in a row and seem to be coming into strong form.
"It doesn't mean anything, we have to continue, because five games for us is nothing, we want to win every game," added Mbappe, 27.
"(Winning) is a good message today, but we can't think the season is done -- next week (at Racing) Santander we have to put in the same intensity."

item.title: Inter rally late to down Fiorentina and regain Serie A lead
item.description:
Inter Milan struck twice in stoppage time to complete a remarkable 2-1 comeback win over Fiorentina at San Siro on Sunday and return to the summit of Serie A.
Alex Jimenez's rocket strike had the struggling visitors heading for a shock win, but Marcus Thuram levelled in the 91st minute before winning a penalty that Piotr Zielinski converted in the 98th minute.
The result meant the Nerazzurri returned to first place, level with surprise fellow pace-setters Lazio on 22 points, while the Florence club's winless run stretched to four games to keep them in 18th spot.
It was Inter's fifth comeback win of the season, while they conceded for the 10th time, but head coach Cristian Chivu was unconcerned by his side's defensive issues.
"That's football: sometimes you concede," Chivu told DAZN. "The important thing is not to let your heads drop and to maintain the same mentality. Ever since I arrived here, I've always said that games last 90 minutes."
"I don't want to see people feel sorry for themselves," Chivu added. "I want to see players respond to setbacks."
Chivu's side had the better of the first half but could not find a way past David de Gea, who made a fingertip stop on a Pio Esposito header before showing quick reactions to parry Thuram's angled drive.
De Gea was alert again to parry a fierce Thuram strike over the bar early in the second half, but it was the visitors who struck first against the run of play after 65 minutes.
Former AC Milan player Jimenez took debutant Inter goalkeeper Ivan Provedel by surprise with an audacious angled strike from distance that flew into the top corner.
Inter piled forward in search of an equaliser, with Carlos Augusto's glancing header coming off the top of the bar and De Gea denying substitute Petar Sucic, but they could not find a way through until the game was into added time.
Thuram guided a shot into the bottom corner to level the scores before winning a penalty when he was dragged down by Victor Valdepenas in the box, which Zielinski converted to complete a pulsating victory.
There was an eight-goal thriller in Bergamo as Atalanta and Frosinone played out a 4-4 draw in which both sides came from behind twice, extending La Dea's winless run to three games in all competitions and keeping the visitors in sixth place.
Genoa claimed a 1-0 win at home to Venezia thanks to a goal from Mikael Ellertsson to climb up to 16th place as Davide Nicola's side stayed bottom.
Later on Sunday, Juventus travel to Lecce before AC Milan go to Udinese.

item.title: Carrick on the brink as Utd misery mounts, Isak stars for Liverpool
item.description:
Michael Carrick was pushed to the brink of being sacked after Manchester United slumped to a miserable 3-0 home defeat against Bournemouth, while Alexander Isak extended his hot streak in Liverpool's 2-0 win against Brighton on Sunday.
Carrick's bold decision to drop captain Bruno Fernandes backfired as defeat stretched United's winless run to eight games and left them 16th in the Premier League, just one point above the relegation zone.
For the third time in four seasons, the Cherries won by a three-goal margin at Old Trafford as strikes from Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson secured a fully deserved victory for Marco Rose's side.
Fernandes was critical of Carrick's tactics in a 4-1 Champions League thrashing at Como on Wednesday.
The United boss said the decision to leave out last season's Premier League Player of the Year was a "purely football" driven, but it was hard to believe Fernandes was not being punished as he was left on the bench for the entire match.
Carrick was taunted with chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning" from the Bournemouth fans.
But on this evidence, dismissing another manager is far from a quick fix for a club that has fallen dramatically from grace since Alex Ferguson's retirement after winning their most recent English title 13 years ago.
A strong finish to last season during Carrick's interim spell in charge secured third place in the Premier League.
Yet with just one win against promoted Ipswich, United have taken just seven points from eight league games so far this season -- their lowest tally at this stage of a season since 1986-87.
United's players were booed off by the few frustrated fans that remained inside Old Trafford at the end of their heaviest home defeat since 2024.
United's co-owners the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe were also targeted for angry chants, although Carrick largely avoided the fans' ire.
It is unlikely that sympathy vote will spare the former United midfielder from the axe.
At Anfield, Liverpool struck twice in quick succession in the first half, with Pascal Gross's own goal followed by Isak's latest strike.
Isak has netted six times in seven league games this season and has three goals in his last four matches.
After a turbulent debut season following his acrimonious move from Newcastle, the Sweden striker is finally beginning to repay his £125 million ($167 million) fee.
It was a welcome first taste of top-flight success at Anfield for Reds boss Andoni Iraola, who had failed to win his first three league games on Merseyside since arriving from Bournemouth in the close season.
The Spaniard, who had won Champions League and League Cup games at Anfield, has led Liverpool to four successive victories in all competitions since the chastening 3-0 home defeat against Manchester City.
Liverpool have climbed to fourth place, just one point behind third-placed Brighton after inflicting the high-flying Seagulls' second league loss this term.
The rampant Reds are six points behind leaders City as they eye a potential title challenge.
William Osula and Harvey Barnes scored in the second half as Newcastle piled pressure on Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage with a 2-0 win at Selhurst Park.
Thrashed 5-0 at rivals Brighton last weekend, 17th-placed Palace have won just twice in eight league games under Sage, who arrived from Lens in the close season to replace Oliver Glasner.
Hull's unbeaten home record remains intact but the Tigers have not tasted victory for seven games after a 1-1 draw with Brentford at the MKM Stadium.
Oli McBurnie's 24th-minute penalty, awarded when Aaron Hickey fouled Tim Iroegbunam, put Hull ahead, but Dango Ouattara equalised in the 63rd minute.

item.title: Mbappe double helps Real stun Barca in La Liga Clasico
item.description:
Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid a 2-1 Clasico victory over La Liga leaders Barcelona on Sunday at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points.
French superstar Mbappe opened the scoring before the interval and then slotted home late on to inflict Barca's first domestic defeat of the campaign after Raphinha had equalised for the champions.
Real Madrid remain third, behind Atletico Madrid and Hansi Flick's Barca, who had won their first nine games before a chastening week.
The Catalans suffered a second straight defeat after losing on Tuesday against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League.
Mourinho was delighted with his team's display in his first Clasico back at the helm of Madrid.
"My team had an extraordinary game, very organised, good concentration, with courage to play out from the back against a team that presses you a lot," Mourinho told reporters.
"We had chances for the second goal... obviously Barca had a strong reaction but we were calm and organised and at 1-1 we never lost our tranquility."
Barca had won six of the seven previous Clasicos since Flick arrived but were surprisingly subdued against Mourinho's side.
"You saw today, we lacked freshness," said Flick of his team's performance.
"It's the first defeat in La Liga, we won nine in a row. This is what we have to see.
"Defeats are a part of the game. We have to analyse, we have to make things better. Now it's important that we make a reaction."
Los Blancos, without suspended winger Vinicius Junior, won their fifth straight game across all competitions and are finding their footing under veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho.
After two trophyless seasons Madrid turned back to Mourinho to try and stop Barca's dominance, and this result will give them hope they are on the right track.
The opening period of the game was cagey, with few opportunities.
Barca defender Pau Cubarsi twice reacted well to shut down Mbappe, while Real Madrid's Marc Cucurella took a rapid liking for Lamine Yamal's shirt, constantly grabbing at the 19-year-old winger.
Anthony Gordon, playing in his first Clasico since joining Barcelona from Newcastle, backheeled the ball to Raphinha, who fired narrowly wide as Barca threatened.
The hosts were dealt a setback when young defender Xavi Espart pulled up hurt and needed to be replaced by Alejandro Balde before the half-hour mark.
Andriy Lunin, playing in goal for Madrid after Thibaut Courtois pulled out of the squad with flu, saved at his near post from Gordon before the visitors took the lead.
Mbappe scored his 10th league goal of the season and also his easiest, with Barca's Gerard Martin clearing a cross straight at the Frenchman, who deflected it into the net.
Barca responded by carving out a glorious chance for an equaliser but teenage sensation Yamal for once miscued in front of goal, firing wide when poised to level.
The game opened up and Yan Diomande came close to doubling Madrid's lead before half-time, drilling into the side-netting.
Martin redeemed himself early in the second half as he held off Jude Bellingham, who could neither beat the defender nor find a free Mbappe.
Raphinha, who had a quiet first half, pulled Barcelona level just after the hour mark.
Pedri fed the Brazilian, La Liga's top goalscorer with 13, who fired through Bellingham's legs and Lunin could not keep the shot out.
The Ukrainian goalkeeper did make a superb save to deny Martin at a corner, as Barcelona flowed forward with the wind finally in their sails.
Yamal bent an effort wide with Lunin at full stretch and Barca substitute Frenkie de Jong had a shot desperately blocked by Dean Huijsen.
There was a sting in the tail for the Catalans though as substitute Gabriel Jesus lost possession and Madrid raced through on goal.
Eduardo Camavinga beat Cubarsi and unselfishly cut the ball back for Mbappe to tuck home his second of the night into an empty net with Joan Garcia drawn out of position.
It brought up a century of goals since Mbappe joined Madrid from PSG in 2024, although the trophies to match have not yet followed.
"(Winning) is a good message today, but we can't think the season is done -- next week (at Racing) Santander we have to put in the same intensity," Mbappe told Real Madrid TV.
